identity.title: ALMA Survey of Orion Planck Galactic Cold Clumps (ALMASOP): Deriving Inclination Angle and Velocity of the Protostellar Jets from Their SiO Knots

paper_type_evidence.quote: We have selected six sources (G209.55-19.68S2, G205.46-14.56S1$_{-}$A, G203.21-11.20W2, G191.90-11.21S, G205.46-14.56S3, and G206.93-16.61W2) from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array Survey of Orion Planck Galactic Cold Clumps (ALMASOP), in which these sources have been mapped in the CO (J=2-1), SiO (J=5-4), and C$^{18}$O (J=2-1) lines.

question.value: Can a shock-forming model of semi-periodical jet velocity variations derive the inclination angle and velocity of protostellar jets from single-epoch ALMA observations of SiO knots?

findings_qualitative.value: Four of the six jets (G209, G205, G203, and G191) are monopolar in both SiO and high-velocity CO on the redshifted side, while their low-velocity CO outflows are bipolar.

evidence.loc: SiO jets and the shock-forming model
evidence.quote: Notice that four of the jets (G209, G205, G203, and G191) happen to be monopolar jets in both SiO and CO and are seen only on the redshifted side, and the other two jets (G205S3 and G206) are bipolar.
In our sample, four of the jets detected in SiO are monopolar and are seen only on the redshifted side, although their associated CO outflows are bipolar.

findings_qualitative.value: There is a gap without SiO emission between the central source and the first knot in four of the jets, explained by the catch-up distance required to form internal shocks.

evidence.loc: SiO jets and the shock-forming model
evidence.quote: Interestingly, there is no SiO emission between the central sources and their first (closest) knots in four of the jets.

findings_qualitative.value: A clear majority of the analyzed jet knot sources have velocity variation periods on the order of decades and show evidence of multi-year mid-IR or sub-mm accretion variability.

evidence.quote: It is striking that the majority of jets analyzed in this paper have knot timescales on the order of decades (Table [1](#tab-params)), suggesting that there is some recurrent form of disk or accretion instability operating at this frequency.

claims.hypothesis: The inclination angle and velocity of protostellar jets can be derived from single-epoch observations of SiO knots using a shock-forming model of semi-periodical jet velocity variations.
claims.experiment: Measured knot distances (D_obs), intervals (Delta D_obs), radial sideways-ejection velocities (Delta V_obs), and radial jet velocities (V_obs) in six ALMASOP jets to compute jet inclinations, and compared them with CO outflow inclinations derived from a wide-angle wind-driven shell model.
claims.result: Derived SiO jet inclination angles (1.0 to 52 deg) are broadly consistent within errors with the CO outflow inclination angles (2 to 40 deg).
claims.finding: The consistency between jet and outflow inclination angles supports that the shock-forming model can be used to derive the inclination angle and velocity of the jets.

evidence.quote: As can be seen from Table [2](#tab:CO), the inclination angles derived for the jets, $i(\rm SiO)$, using the shock-forming model are broadly consistent (within the errors) with those derived for the associated outflows, $i(\rm CO)$, using the wind-driven shell model.
Thus, this consistency supports that the shock-forming model can be used to derive the inclination angle and velocity of the jets.

claims.hypothesis: The shock-forming model reproduces jet velocities and inclination angles measured independently via multi-epoch proper motion studies.
claims.experiment: Applied the shock-forming model to three previously reported SiO jets in the literature (HH 211, HH 212, and L1448C(N)) that have independent proper motion and radial velocity measurements.
claims.result: Model-derived inclinations and velocities (HH 211: 10 deg, 114 km s^-1; HH 212: 3 deg, 141 km s^-1; L1448C(N): 36 and 59 deg, 92 and 71 km s^-1) agree within uncertainties with proper-motion values (HH 211: 11 deg, 104 km s^-1; HH 212: 4 deg, 115 km s^-1; L1448C(N): 40 deg, 88 km s^-1).
claims.finding: The shock-forming model accurately determines jet velocity and inclination angle from SiO knots, supporting that the knots are produced by semi-periodical variations in jet velocity.

evidence.quote: As can be seen in Table 1, the derived inclination angle and velocity of the jet in these three jets are also broadly consistent with those previously measured from proper motion and radial velocity.

Our results support that the knots in the jets are indeed produced by semi-periodical variations in jet velocity, so that the shock-forming model can be used to determine the velocity and inclination angle of the jets from the SiO knots.

why_this_data.value: The six sources were selected from the ALMASOP survey because they were the only ones showing clear periodical knotty structures in their SiO jets.

evidence.quote: The data are part of the ALMA Survey of Orion Planck Galactic Cold Clumps (ALMASOP) project (cite: 2020ApJ...898..107H; 2020ApJS..251...20D; 2021ApJ...907L..15S), in which only these six targeted sources were seen with clear periodical knotty structures.

why_this_method.value: Direct measurement of jet velocity via proper motion requires multi-epoch observations over several years, whereas the shock-forming model constrains both inclination angle and jet velocity from a single epoch of observation.

evidence.quote: However, it requires multi-epoch observations with enough spatial and velocity resolution over several years to measure the jet proper motion in order to derive the jet velocity. In addition, inclination angle of the jet, which is also needed to derive the jet velocity, can not be measured directly. Here we employ a novel method to constrain both the inclination angle and the jet velocity, requiring only one epoch of observation.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Periodical enhanced mass ejections as the origin of the knots (considered unlikely because it is unclear how such ejections can form shocks to produce SiO emission)

evidence.quote: Alternatively, the knots could be due to periodical enhanced mass ejections. However, it is unclear how such ejections can form shocks (cite: 2014prpl.conf..451F) to produce the observed SiO knotty shocks.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Asymmetry of ambient material as the cause of monopolar SiO/CO jets (rejected because ambient material can only affect low-velocity CO outflow material)

evidence.quote: This asymmetry of the jets is unlikely to be caused by an asymmetry of the ambient material, which can only affect material at low velocity in the CO outflow (cite: 2014A&A...563L...3C).

limitations_admitted.value: The distance where the shock first forms (D_obs) is uncertain.

evidence.loc: SiO jets and the shock-forming model
evidence.quote: Here the distance where the shock first forms $D_{\rm obs}$ is uncertain and is thus assumed to have an error of $0.5 \Delta D_{\rm obs}$ on the negative side and a half of the beam size on the positive side,

limitations_admitted.value: For the shock-forming model to work, jets must have at least a few roughly equally spaced knots produced by internal shocks, shock speed around 10 to 40 km s^-1, and no significant energy dissipation in the shocks.

evidence.quote: Notice that, in order for this model to work, the jets must have at least a few roughly equally spaced knots produced by internal shocks. In addition, the shock speed ($\Delta V$) should be around 10 to 40 km s$^{-1}$ (cite: 1997A&A...321..293S), so that the SiO emission is indeed produced by shocks. Moreover, no significant energy is dissipated in the shocks so that the thermal energy produced by the shocks can be totally transferred sideways into the sideways ejection.

limitations_admitted.value: Further observations at a larger scale are needed to check whether asymmetry in the ambient material causes the opening angle asymmetry of the CO outflows.

evidence.quote: Some asymmetry is seen in the ambient material in the C$^{18}$O total intensity maps around the sources (Figure [2](#outflow) (a) to (d)), however, further observations at a larger scale are needed to check it.

referee_caveats_inferred: The assumption of zero radiative/thermal energy dissipation in internal shocks (so that sideways expansion velocity strictly equals the velocity variation amplitude Delta V) is an idealized approximation for radiative protostellar shocks.

Subjective exclusion of the innermost knots in several sources (G205S3 blue, G206, HH 211, L1448C(N)) as having a 'different origin' directly alters D_obs and therefore the derived inclination and velocity.
The values of Delta V_obs in Table 1 are rounded to 20, 30, or 40 km s^-1 without quoted measurement uncertainties, so uncertainty in Delta V_obs is not propagated into i and V_j.

reproducibility.score_reason: The ALMA project code (2018.1.00302.S) is public, basic imaging parameters (CASA 5.4, tclean, robust 0.5, velocity resolution, beam, rms) are stated, and the analytical equations for both the shock-forming model and wind-driven shell model are fully given alongside all intermediate measured quantities in Table 1. reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: Public ALMA data (2018.1.00302.S) and a simple, explicit analytical recipe (Equations 1-12) with full intermediate and final numerical tables (Tables 1 and 2) make this a strong candidate for reproducing both the image-plane knot measurements and the derived kinematic parameters.
